h1: Worm tubs versus shell and tube condensers
title: Worm Tubs or Shell and Tube Condensers | Craft Beer School
desc: How worm tubs and shell and tube condensers differ on a pot still: copper contact, spirit weight, cooling water and what suits a hot climate.
teaser: The condenser is the last part of the still the spirit touches. Its design can make the new make light or meaty.
standfirst: Pot stills end in a condenser, where vapour turns back into liquid. The old worm tub and the modern shell and tube condenser do the same job very differently. The new make tastes the difference.
sections: Two ways to turn vapour into spirit

Every pot still needs a condenser at the end of the lyne arm. Hot alcohol vapour goes in, cooling water takes the heat away and liquid distillate comes out. There are two main designs on malt whisky stills. A worm tub is a long coiled copper pipe, the worm, sitting in a large tub of cold water. A shell and tube condenser is a cylinder filled with many narrow copper tubes, with cooling water flowing through the tubes and vapour condensing in the space around them.

Both condense the spirit. The difference lies in how much copper the vapour touches on the way.
Worm tubs give less copper contact

In a worm tub the vapour enters one wide pipe and condenses quickly as the coil cools it. Once it is liquid, it has far less reactive contact with the copper. The total copper surface is also smaller than in a shell and tube unit of the same capacity. So less sulphur is removed.

The result is a heavier new make, often described as meaty, sulphury or robust. Distilleries that use worm tubs usually do so on purpose, for that weight. Sulphur fades over years in cask. The heavier spirit can develop depth. Our guide to copper contact and spirit character explains why copper matters so much.
Shell and tube condensers give more

A shell and tube condenser spreads vapour over a large area of copper tubing. Vapour stays in contact with copper as it condenses over a large surface. More sulphur is removed. The new make is usually lighter and cleaner, with fruit and floral notes more prominent.

Shell and tube condensers are also compact, efficient and easier to control. They are the standard choice on most modern pot stills. Stillmen can adjust cooling water flow to change condensing behaviour. Some distilleries run warmer condenser water to increase copper contact further.
Cooling water is the hidden cost

A worm tub holds a large volume of water and needs it cold. Traditionally, worm tubs sat outside and were fed by cold streams. As the tub water warms during a run, condensing becomes less efficient and must be managed with fresh cold water. A shell and tube condenser uses water more efficiently and can work with a cooling tower or chiller loop.

Cooling water temperature affects both designs. Water that is too warm risks vapour passing through uncondensed, which is a safety and yield problem. Our guide to cooling water for condensers in a hot climate covers the plant side.

India's climate pushes hard on this choice. Mains or borewell water can arrive at 28 to 32 °C in summer, far warmer than a Scottish stream. A worm tub relies on a large volume of cold water, so keeping it cold here means chillers or a large cooling tower working hard. A shell and tube condenser on a chilled water loop is usually the more practical choice for a new craft distillery.

A worm tub is still possible if you want its heavy style. Budget for chilling, plan for heat load in April and May and accept higher running costs. Make that decision knowing what it costs, rather than discovering it in the first summer.

Condenser choice works together with still shape. A tall still with a rising lyne arm and a shell and tube condenser stacks the odds towards a light spirit. A short still with a falling lyne arm and a worm tub stacks them towards a heavy one. Mixing features gives an in-between result. Some distilleries even switch between condenser types to make two styles.

The condenser is the last piece of copper the spirit touches before the spirit safe. Choosing it well means seeing the whole still and the plant's cooling supply as one design, which is where a structured course pays for itself.

Measure the temperature of your available cooling water at mid afternoon in May. Write it on the same page as the spirit style you want. Take both numbers to your still fabricator and ask for condenser options sized for that water temperature. If the answer assumes 15 °C water, it was designed for somewhere else.
faqs: What is a worm tub on a whisky still?
A long coiled copper pipe sitting in a tub of cold water. Vapour from the still condenses as it passes through the coil.
Do worm tubs make heavier whisky?
Generally, yes. They give less copper contact than shell and tube condensers, so more sulphur remains and the new make is heavier.
Why are shell and tube condensers more common?
They are compact, efficient and easy to control. They also give more copper contact for a cleaner spirit.
Which condenser is better for a distillery in a hot climate?
A shell and tube condenser on a chilled water loop is usually more practical, because worm tubs need a large volume of cold water.
